[THOUGHT] The patient is an adolescent with a ~1-year history of slowly enlarging, well-demarcated depigmented macules/patches on the lateral back. Lesions are described as depigmented (complete loss of pigment) rather than merely hypopigmented, and there is uncertainty about scaling; KOH prep from an active edge was normal (no fungal elements), making tinea versicolor unlikely. Nevus depigmentosus is typically congenital and stable rather than progressively enlarging in adolescence. Postinflammatory hypopigmentation would usually follow a prior inflammatory event. The clinical picture — acquired, progressive, well-demarcated depigmented macules in a 15-year-old with negative KOH — is most consistent with vitiligo (acquired idiopathic leukoderma), which commonly presents in childhood/adolescence and slowly enlarges over time. Therefore vitiligo is the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Vitiligo (acquired, nonsegmental leukoderma)

[THOUGHT] The history and exam are most consistent with vitiligo: a 15-year-old with several well-demarcated depigmented macules/patches on the trunk that have been slowly expanding over a year. A negative KOH makes tinea versicolor unlikely (and the patient is unsure about scaling). Key differentials to consider include tinea versicolor (KOH usually positive), post‑inflammatory hypopigmentation, nevus depigmentosus (congenital), halo nevus, and—rarely—paucisymptomatic leprosy (would have sensory change). Vitiligo is primarily a clinical diagnosis and the described lesions (depigmented, well-demarcated, progressive) are characteristic.

Red-flag or useful missing data: Wood’s lamp exam (to accentuate depigmentation), presence/absence of sensory changes in lesions (to exclude leprosy), distribution symmetry and involvement of mucosa/nails/hair, onset (congenital vs acquired), and pertinent personal/family autoimmune history (thyroid disease). These are useful but not strictly required to make an initial clinical diagnosis.

[DECISION] PASS
